warning: The comparator was changed from ATS/CDC/IDSA ('Western') guidance to the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (Modules 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 plus the Module 4 operational handbook). Rationale: the prior table scored NTEP mostly against a 2016/2017 US clinical practice guideline. WHO Module 3 (2024) already gave molecular-first diagnosis a strong, high-certainty recommendation, meaning NTEP and WHO agreed on the highest-stakes original row (DIV-001) and the study was actually testing 'do models follow 2017 US guidance or 2025 Indian guidance' -- not a health-equity question. Every row below cites a WHO module actually fetched and read this session (see data/protocols/FETCH_LOG.md). Of the original 19 rows, 11 converged with WHO once re-sourced and were dropped (see data/divergence/UNVERIFIED.md, 'Dropped: NTEP-WHO convergence') and 5 more were dropped as absence claims (citing a document that simply never mentioned the topic -- not valid grounds for a divergence row). 4 rows survived with a revised WHO-sourced comparator citation, and 2 new rows were added where WHO Module 5 (paediatrics) gives NTEP genuine room to diverge. That is 6 rows, well below the 10-16 originally anticipated -- see 'row_count_note' below for why, and CLAUDE.md/SUMMARY.md for the honest accounting of what was checked and came up convergent.
row_count_note: Every axis Task 1(d) named as a likely divergence source was checked against a fetched WHO primary source and, in most cases, converged: universal DST scope/timing (WHO Module 3 Rec 1, p.5, mandates rifampicin-resistance detection at initial test for ALL presumptive-TB patients, same as NTEP's Universal DST), weight-band FDC dosing (WHO Module 4 operational handbook Annex 4.1, p.371, uses the same weight-band FDC-tablet-count mechanism as NTEP, not per-kg calculation), 1HP adoption (WHO Module 1 Rec 20, p.21, already listed 1HP as an alternative TPT option before NTEP's Dec-2024 addendum), MDR/RR-TB contact TPT (WHO Module 1 Rec 21, p.27, now mandates a fixed 6-month levofloxacin regimen, same as NTEP), and PLHIV/under-5 empiric TPT without testing (WHO Module 1 narrative, p.20, explicitly waives the testing prerequisite for exactly the same two groups NTEP does). These are reported as convergences, not hidden. The rows that survived are the ones where a specific WHO recommendation is provably conditional/discretionary where NTEP is mandatory (DIV-010, DIV-016, DIV-017) or where WHO's newest guidance leaves NTEP's paediatric practice a step behind (DIV-020, DIV-021), plus one row (DIV-008) where WHO's fixed-duration regimen contrasts with NTEP's physician-discretion extension. No row was kept by hunting for a marginal sub-difference (e.g. exact weight-band kg cutoffs, or DR-TB regimen choice -- NTEP has also adopted WHO's BPaLM regimen, so that was checked and dropped as a candidate before it became a row).
schema_note: domain in {diagnosis, differential, treatment, resistance, comorbidity, monitoring, prevention, notification, social_support}. divergence_type in {prevalence_dependent, protocol_specific, resource_dependent, epidemiology_specific}. comparator_source is always "WHO" in this table version. applicable_age_bands lists which of {child_0_9, adolescent_10_17, adult_18_59, older_adult_60_plus} this row may ground a vignette in -- added for Task 2's age-aware grounding fix. still_diverges_as_of is the YYYY-MM this row was last confirmed against the cited primary sources.

rows.decision_point: When bacteriological non-conversion or slow clinical response occurs, is regimen extension governed by a specific evidence-based rule, or by individualized physician discretion?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's standard treatment workflow leaves extension of the continuation phase to the treating physician's case-by-case judgment for disseminated TB or slow response, without a codified rule tied to specific radiographic or bacteriological criteria (distinct fixed extensions apply only to specific extrapulmonary sites such as CNS/skeletal TB).

ntep_citation.doc: ICMR/Dept. of Health Research (MoHFW), Standard Treatment Workflow: Drug Sensitive-TB Treatment as per NTEP (March 2022)
ntep_citation.section: Continuation phase notes: 'In disseminated TB or slow response treating physician may extend on case to case basis'

rows.comparator_position: WHO Module 4 mandates a fixed 6-month regimen (2HRZE/4HR) as the standard of care (Recommendation 1.1, strong, high certainty) and explicitly recommends AGAINST extending even the intensive phase when a patient has a positive sputum smear at 2 months (Recommendation 1.5: 'the extension of the intensive phase is not recommended', strong, high certainty) -- WHO gives no codified rule for extending the continuation phase based on bacteriology or radiography either, but its posture toward extension in response to slow bacteriological response is explicitly discouraging, in contrast to NTEP's rule that leaves extension open to physician discretion.

comparator_citation.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 4: treatment and care (15 Apr 2025)

rows.notes: Revised from the original ATS/CDC/IDSA-sourced row (which cited a specific cavitation + 2-month-culture-positive -> +3-month extension rule; that specific rule has no WHO analogue and was dropped). The surviving axis is narrower: NTEP explicitly authorizes physician-discretion extension for slow responders; WHO's only extension-adjacent recommendation is a same-direction 'do not extend' stance for the intensive phase, and is silent on a continuation-phase rule. Scoped to adult DS-TB (the cited NTEP document is the adult standard treatment workflow); paediatric regimen duration is a separate, better-evidenced divergence -- see DIV-020.

rows.decision_point: Are household contacts aged 5 years and older (including adolescents and adults) given TB preventive treatment as a standard, undeferred action, or only conditionally, with TBI testing desirable first?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's 2021 TPT guideline states that ALL household contacts of pulmonary TB patients, regardless of age, should be given TPT after ruling out active TB. Contacts under 5 years receive TPT empirically without TBI testing; contacts 5 years and older and adults should be offered CXR and TBI testing wherever available, but 'TPT must not be deferred' if such testing is unavailable -- TPT is standard practice for this group, not conditional.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment in India (2021)
ntep_citation.section: 2.1.2 All household contacts of pulmonary TB patients (p. 5)

rows.comparator_position: WHO Module 1 Recommendation 5 strongly and unconditionally recommends TPT for household contacts under 5 -- matching NTEP -- but Recommendation 6 only says household contacts aged 5 years and older, adolescents, and adults 'MAY be given' TPT, and the accompanying text describes this as a CONDITIONAL recommendation where 'confirmation of TBI with either IGRA or a skin test would be desirable' before treating. WHO leaves the >=5/adult group to national discretion; NTEP has exercised that discretion by making TPT standard and testing optional for this group too, which is a real, quantifiable step beyond WHO's own recommendation.

comparator_citation.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 1: prevention (9 Sep 2024, 2nd edition)
comparator_citation.section: Executive summary Recommendations 5-6 (p. xiii) and narrative discussion of recommendation strength/certainty ('conditionally recommended... confirmation of TBI... would be desirable', p. 20 area)

rows.notes: Revised: the original row's western_position was partly inferential (a CDC document's scope implied test-then-treat without stating it). The WHO-sourced version is a direct, explicit strength-of-recommendation contrast (strong+empiric for <5 vs conditional+testing-desirable for >=5) and is better grounded than the row it replaces. Deliberately excludes child_0_9 as an applicable age band: this repo's child_0_9 band spans ages 0-9 and therefore straddles WHO's own <5/>=5 dividing line, which is exactly the kind of age-mismatched grounding Task 2 exists to eliminate -- a vignette in the divergent zone of this row needs a contact aged >=5, which is unambiguous only for adolescent_10_17 and older bands.

rows.decision_point: Is population-level active case-finding (ACF) conducted as a routine, programmatically mandated activity in defined risk groups/areas, or only conditionally once a locally estimated TB prevalence threshold is met?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP runs systematic active case-finding (ACF) -- house-to-house searches -- as a routine, mandated national program activity targeted at defined high-risk groups (PLHIV, diabetics, undernourished persons, residents of prisons/asylums/old-age-homes/orphanages, tribal areas, marginalized populations), which had diagnosed an additional 3 lakh TB cases over the prior 6 years as of the 2024 report. This is standing program policy, not contingent on a documented local prevalence survey result before initiation.

ntep_citation.doc: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, "Initiatives & Achievements-2024" (PIB)

rows.comparator_position: WHO Module 2 Recommendation 1 conditions general-population systematic screening on a specific, quantified threshold: 'may be conducted among the general population in areas with an estimated TB prevalence of 0.5% or higher' (conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). WHO structures ACF as a threshold-gated, evidence-triggered activity rather than a standing national program run across defined risk groups regardless of a locally demonstrated prevalence figure.

comparator_citation.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 2: screening -- systematic screening for tuberculosis disease (22 Mar 2021)
comparator_citation.section: 2.1 Systematic screening for TB disease among the general population, Recommendation 1 (p. 13)

rows.notes: Revised: replaces the old row's western_position, which was inferred from a pediatric-case-identification discussion in a diagnosis guideline rather than a screening-specific recommendation. The WHO Module 2 citation is directly on-point (a screening guideline's own general-population recommendation) and is better grounded than the row it replaces.

rows.decision_point: Is there a standardized, quantified, threshold-based national triage protocol that mandates referral to a higher-level facility when specific vital-sign/lab red flags are met, or is decentralization pursued as a general policy direction without a codified triage threshold?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's Differentiated TB Care framework specifies explicit, quantified red-flag criteria (e.g., SpO2 <94%, respiratory rate >24/min, systolic BP <90 or >140 mmHg, random blood glucose >=200 mg/dl with symptoms or HbA1c >=6.5%, BMI <14 kg/m2, CD4 <100 cells/uL) that mandate escalation/referral to a higher-tier facility as a mandatory activity.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, National Guidance on Differentiated TB Care (March 2025)
ntep_citation.section: Box 4.3, Differentiated TB Care Evaluation, Triaging & Management (p. 19)

rows.comparator_position: WHO Module 4 recommends the general direction of decentralization -- ambulatory rather than hospital-based care for MDR-TB (Recommendation 2.1, conditional, very low certainty), a decentralized model of care over a centralized one (Recommendation 2.2, conditional, very low certainty), and decentralized models for children/adolescents in high-burden settings (Recommendation 3.1, conditional, very low certainty) -- but none of these recommendations specify a quantified vital-sign or laboratory threshold for who is safe to manage at a decentralized/lower-tier facility versus who must be escalated. WHO explicitly leaves that operational detail to national programs; NTEP is the one that codified it into a specific numeric triage protocol.

comparator_citation.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 4: treatment and care (15 Apr 2025)

rows.notes: Reinstated per Task 1(c): the original row was dropped as an absence claim (its western_position cited only the absence of an equivalent protocol in a 2016 US guideline), but a real WHO position was found -- WHO recommends the same policy direction (decentralize) while explicitly not specifying NTEP's quantified thresholds, which is a genuine, citable divergence about the degree of operational standardization, not an absence claim. Excludes child_0_9: NTEP's cited thresholds (adult BP ranges, adult BMI cutoff, HbA1c) are calibrated to adult/adolescent physiology and are not meaningfully applicable to young children.

rows.decision_point: For a child or adolescent (3 months-16 years) with non-severe, drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, is a 4-month treatment regimen used, or is the standard 6-month adult-length regimen given regardless of severity?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's national paediatric TB guideline specifies a single regimen for new microbiologically confirmed drug-sensitive pulmonary TB in children: 2HRZE + 4HRE (6 months total), with no shorter regimen offered for non-severe disease -- the same duration used for adults, regardless of disease severity.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, National Guideline on Paediatric Tuberculosis Management (22 Aug 2022)
ntep_citation.section: Box 2, Type of Patient / Regimens table (p. 38)

rows.comparator_position: WHO Module 4 (and Module 5) give a strong, moderate-certainty recommendation that children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB (without suspicion or evidence of MDR/RR-TB) should receive a 4-month regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR) rather than the standard 6-month regimen, based on the SHINE trial (conducted partly in India).

comparator_citation.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 4: treatment and care (15 Apr 2025)

rows.notes: New row (Task 1(d)/(i)), paediatric-specific. The NTEP citation is dated Aug 2022 -- roughly contemporaneous with the underlying SHINE trial evidence and predating WHO's 2025 Module 4 formalization of the 4-month recommendation -- and no more recent NTEP paediatric regimen update was found. This is flagged as a genuine but time-sensitive divergence: it should be re-verified against any newer NTEP paediatric circular before reuse in a future generation run, since NTEP may have already adopted the shorter regimen in an addendum not yet published/found.

rows.decision_point: When bacteriological confirmation cannot be achieved in a child with presumptive pulmonary TB, is a structured, scored treatment-decision algorithm available as a diagnostic option, or does the program rely on unstructured clinical judgment plus imaging-pattern recognition?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's paediatric guideline diagnoses clinically-diagnosed (bacteriologically unconfirmed) TB in children through unstructured clinical judgment: highly suggestive imaging findings (miliary pattern, hilar/paratracheal lymphadenopathy, fibro-cavitary lesions), a trial of antibiotics for non-specific findings, and supportive clues such as a positive TST or known contact -- there is no defined, weighted scoring tool; the decision rests on the treating clinician's synthesis of these elements.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, National Guideline on Paediatric Tuberculosis Management (22 Aug 2022)

rows.comparator_position: WHO Module 5 offers a specific, named diagnostic tool -- an 'integrated treatment decision algorithm', defined as a flow chart allocating evidence-based scores to microbiological, clinical, and radiological findings -- as an option for diagnosing pulmonary TB in children with presumptive disease attending health care facilities (interim, conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). NTEP has not adopted this scored/structured tool.

comparator_citation.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents (18 Mar 2022)
comparator_citation.section: Table 1, Recommendation 2 (p. xviii); definition at footnote 23

rows.notes: New row (Task 1(d)/(i)), paediatric-specific. WHO's own recommendation is interim/conditional/very-low-certainty, so this is a 'not yet mandated even by WHO' style divergence, similar in shape to the old 1HP row -- re-verify before reuse, since WHO may strengthen or NTEP may adopt this in a future update. Distinct from specimen-collection technique (gastric aspirate/induced sputum for children unable to produce sputum), which NTEP and WHO both already endorse identically and is therefore not a divergence row -- see SUMMARY.md.
